title: Understanding Weak Forms and Linking in English

blocks.text: Have you ever noticed how native speakers of English often pronounce function words differently in conversation? This phenomenon is known as weak forms, and it plays a crucial role in fluent speech.

blocks.markdown: Weak forms are reduced pronunciations of function words that occur in connected speech. Common function words such as 'and', 'of', 'to', and 'can' often change their pronunciation when they are not stressed. For example, 'and' is often pronounced as /ən/ instead of /ænd/.

blocks.title: What are Weak Forms?
blocks.text: Weak forms are the reduced pronunciations of function words that occur in fluent speech, making them less prominent than content words.

blocks.markdown: In connected speech, function words often lose their full vowel sounds and are pronounced more quickly. This reduction helps maintain the rhythm and flow of spoken English. For instance, 'to' can be pronounced as /tə/ when it precedes a consonant, as in 'I want to go'.

Linking occurs when a final consonant sound of one word connects smoothly with the initial vowel sound of the next word. This is common in phrases like 'turn off' where the 'n' in 'turn' links with the 'o' in 'off', creating a smoother transition.

blocks.title: Identifying Weak Forms and Linking
blocks.prompt: Listen to the sentence: 'I want to go and see her.' Identify the weak forms and linking.

steps.text: Observe the linking between 'go' and 'and' where the 'o' connects with the 'a'.

blocks.answer: The weak forms are 'to' as /tə/ and 'and' as /ən/. The linking occurs between 'go' and 'and'.

blocks.markdown: WAEC tests weak forms in connected speech to assess students' understanding of natural spoken English. Recognizing these forms is essential for effective communication and comprehension.

blocks.title: Tip for WAEC Exams
blocks.text: Pay attention to weak forms and linking in listening exercises. They often appear in comprehension questions.

points: Weak forms are essential for understanding fluent speech in English.
Linking between words enhances the fluidity of spoken language.
